children: MARKET WRAPS
STOCKS: Stocks rose and the Nasdaq Composite closed at a record high as optimism about artificial intelligence offset fears about rising bond yields.
TREASURYS: Yields on 10- and 30-year Treasurys closed at their highest levels since 2002.
FOREX: The U.S. dollar rose against rivals as French budget worries weighed on the euro, sending it to the lowest level compared to the greenback in more than a year.
COMMODITIES: Oil futures fell amid hopes that Middle East supply interruptions would be mitigated by the Group of Seven nations' release of emergency fuel reserves.
HEADLINES
U.S. Services-Sector Activity Continued to Expand in September
U.S. services-sector activity expanded at a slower pace in September,
a survey of managers found.
The Institute for Supply Management's purchasing managers index for
services providers was 54.9 in September, compared with 55.4 in the prior
month. Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal expected a reading of
55. A reading above 50 suggests economic growth, while one below 50
indicates contraction.
The new orders index registered 59.8, compared with 60.9 in the prior
month. The employment index returned to slight expansion after two months
in contraction, the survey said.
Supreme Court Questions Oil Companies' Bid to Shut Down Climate Lawsuits
WASHINGTON-Oil companies seeking to avoid lawsuits over climate change
faced skeptical questions Monday at the Supreme Court, with several
justices expressing doubts about the industry's campaign to shut down
dozens of cases brought by state and local governments.
On the first day of the court's new term, the justices debated whether
communities can seek financial damages for harms allegedly caused by
extreme weather events that scientists say are tied to the worldwide
burning of fossil fuels. Justices across the ideological spectrum noted
that state-based lawsuits are routinely used to target other conduct with
widespread effects, such as the marketing of tobacco, the manufacture of
asbestos or the production of defective automobiles.
"What makes this situation different from all those other ones?" Chief
Justice John Roberts asked a lawyer representing ExxonMobil and Suncor
Energy, which are fighting a lawsuit brought by Boulder, Colo. Similar
lawsuits are pending around the country and threaten the energy industry
with massive financial liability.
Paramount Names Leadership Team for Combined Entity Post $81 Billion
Warner Deal
Paramount Skydance laid out more details of its leadership structure
ahead of the close of its deal for Warner Bros. Discovery, confirming the
positions of David Ellison, Bari Weiss and Mark Thompson.
The appointments, announced Monday, come as Paramount looks to close
its $81 billion deal for Warner this week. A federal judge last week
approved Paramount's settlement with 12 state attorneys general to
resolve an antitrust case, paving the way for the acquisition to close.
David Ellison, CEO of Paramount, will be chairman and chief executive
of the combined company-dubbed Skydance-alongside co-CEO Ynon Kreiz.
Paramount disclosed the appointment of Kreiz, the outgoing CEO of Mattel,
last week.
Schneider Electric to Buy Software Maker PTC for $22.6 Billion
France's Schneider Electric agreed to buy PTC in an all-cash deal that
values the U.S. industrial-software maker at $22.6 billion, moving to
prepare its portfolio for industrial artificial intelligence.
Schneider said Monday that it offered $205 a share in cash for PTC, a
42% premium to its last closing price. PTC's board decided to recommend
that the company's shareholders approve the deal.
Shares in Schneider dropped more than 8% in European morning trading,
while PTC's stock jumped 35% in U.S. premarket exchanges.
C.H. Robinson to Buy RXO for About $5.8 Billion
America's largest freight broker C.H. Robinson Worldwide is buying one
of its biggest rivals, RXO, in a stock-and-cash transaction valued at
$5.8 billion.
C.H. Robinson CEO Dave Bozeman, who has used artificial intelligence
to boost productivity, said the acquisition will expand his company's
expedited and last-mile delivery services. The deal will generate about
$300 million in annual savings within two years of its close, the company
said.
It will make C.H. Robinson the fifth-largest third-party logistics
company in the world by revenue and more than twice as big as its next
biggest competitor in the U.S. domestic freight brokerage sector,
according to market research and consulting group Armstrong & Associates.
GE HealthCare to Buy Sofie for Nearly $1 Billion to Grow Medical-Imaging
Business
GE HealthCare Technologies said Monday it planned to purchase a
manufacturer of radioactive substances used in medical imaging procedures
for $945 million in cash.
The deal marks a continued push by medical-equipment maker GE
HealthCare into the growing market for radiopharmaceuticals, which have
uses for both diagnosing and treating diseases including cancer, heart
disease and Alzheimer's.
Drugmakers such as Novartis and other devicemakers have been investing
in the segment. In August, Curium struck a deal to acquire Lantheus
Holdings for an initial $6.7 billion in a consolidation of two
radiopharma companies.
Texas AG Paxton Launches Investigation Into UnitedHealth Group
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton launched an investigation into
UnitedHealth Group, accusing the healthcare company of illegal practices
that have blocked access to healthcare for Texans.
Paxton has sent civil investigative demands to the company to collect
evidence around potential violations of the Texas Deceptive Trade
Practices Act, according to a Monday statement from his office.
The statement highlighted reports alleging that United bribed nursing
homes to delay hospitalizations for patients, directed and in some cases
denied patient care over physicians' judgement, and retroactively
withdrew its approval of a prior-authorization request for one Texas
patient.
Centalion, Fresh From Rebrand, Does Deal for U.S. Gas Fields
Centalion, the commodities trader formerly known as Gunvor, has bought
a collection of natural-gas assets from Silver Hill Energy Partners in a
deal valued at around $1.5 billion, according to people familiar with the
matter.
The deal is a bet that demand for U.S. gas will keep growing at home
and abroad, fueled by supply disruptions in the Middle East and the
growing power needs of data centers. It will make Centalion a major
player in the Haynesville basin, a prolific gas region straddling Texas
and Louisiana.
The trading firm has done a series of U.S. gas deals under Chief
Executive Gary Pedersen, who replaced co-founder Torbjörn Törnqvist after
an ill-fated attempt last fall to acquire the international operations of
Russia's Lukoil.
Eli Lilly Scores FDA Win for Pancreatic Cancer Drug. How It's Moving
Beyond GLP-1s.
Another day, another chance for Eli Lilly to prove it is more than
just a leader in weight-loss drugs. That validation came in the form of a
regulatory win for its experimental cancer treatment, olomorasib.
The Food and Drug Administration on Monday granted olomorasib orphan
drug designation. The status is reserved for investigational treatments
that target rare, life-threatening diseases affecting fewer than 200,000
people in the U.S.
The move also builds on a decision by the FDA in August, which granted
olomorasib so-called Breakthrough Therapy status as a standalone
treatment for adults with a specific form of pancreatic cancer who have
received at least one prior therapy.

TALKING POINT BofA's Merrill Agrees to $39 Million Settlement Over Low Interest Rates on Retirement Accounts Bank of America's Merrill unit has agreed to pay $39 million to settle a class-action lawsuit against the company for allegedly underpaying interest on certain customers' cash in so-called sweep accounts. The proposed settlement document was filed in court Sept. 30 by attorneys representing both the company and the plaintiff, Merrill Edge customer Sarah Valelly.

The settlement potentially covers customers who had Merrill Edge retirement accounts with cash balances that were swept into low-paying sweep accounts from Dec. 15, 2016 through March 15, 2020, according to the court document. Customers were paid as little as 0.01% in interest on cash, according to the court document. U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni still has to approve the settlement.
A representative for Merrill declined to comment on the case.

Adam J. Blander, an attorney at law firm Wolf Popper which represents Valelly, says his client's cash sweep case has inspired similar legal battles. "We are gratified that Wolf Popper was able to achieve this result after seven years of hard-fought litigation," he says. "Valelly was the first known case to address a broker's contractual obligation to pay a reasonable rate of interest on retirement sweep accounts."

The settlement could bring closure to a seven-year long legal battle in which Valelly accused the company of breach of contract. Her lawsuit, which was filed in federal court in New York in 2019, centered on how the company moved, or swept, some Merrill Edge customers' idle cash into accounts that paid a "paltry" rate of interest that was below prevailing market rates of approximately 2% at the time. The company's client relationship agreement for Merrill Edge self-directed customers promised to pay reasonable rates, according to Valelly's lawsuit.
In February, a federal judge issued an order granting class certification to Valelly's lawsuit. The two sides were due to go to trial later this month, according to the proposed settlement agreement.
Valelly's legal complaint predates other cash sweep lawsuits that have been filed in recent years against other companies such as LPL Financial and Charles Schwab. Those cases are continuing.
Andrew Welsch, Barron's
